# LLP 2000.000: Snapback 3 — keep the core, flip two substrates, start at hub scale

**Type:** RFC
**Status:** Draft
**Role:** Second opinion on LLP 2000; since 2026-09-12 also the design brief Snapback 4 builds (LLP 3000)
**Systems:** Snapback 3 product architecture, bounded computation, client data model, client API vocabulary, language and tooling, effects runtime, verification (simulation), performance budgets, process
**Author:** Claude Fable 5.1, at Charlie Cheever's request
**Date:** 2026-09-12
**Revised:** 2026-09-12 (adopted as the Snapback 4 design brief by LLP 3000 decision 3); 2026-09-12 (initial)
**Related:** [LLP 2000](./2000-snapback3.rfc.md) (parent), [LLP 3000](./3000-snapback4.explainer.md) (the Snapback 4 root that builds this brief), LLP 0000, [LLP 0329](./0329-agent-native-rebuild-diagnosis.research.md), [LLP 0329.014.004](./0329.014.004-bounded-data-programs-v1-design.rfc.md), [LLP 0329.016](./0329.016-agentic-dev-loop-from-scratch.rfc.md), [LLP 1000](./1000-snapback2.explainer.md), [LLP 1001](./1001-query-engine.spec.md), [LLP 1002](./1002-dev-loop.spec.md), [LLP 1012](./1012-local-first-v1.spec.md), [LLP 1018.003](./1018.003-truthful-and-composed-client.decision.md), [LLP 1018.008](./1018.008-elegance-after-the-corrections.research.md), [LLP 1018.008.007](./1018.008.007-affordable-offline-acquisition.research.md), [LLP 1018.008.008](./1018.008.008-locality-of-application-changes.research.md), [LLP 1018.008.009](./1018.008.009-residual-ergonomic-gaps.research.md), [LLP 1019](./1019-derived-delivery-custody.rfc.md), [LLP 1020](./1020-day-two-evolution-and-legible-ceilings.rfc.md), [LLP 1023](./1023-clique-builder-jump.rfc.md), [LLP 1024](./1024-single-lane-delivered-search.rfc.md), [LLP 1025](./1025-digest-final-emission-at-hub-scale.research.md), `rules/RULES.md`, `rules/NOT-DOING.md`, `benchmarks/runs/2026-09-05-clique-full-3x3/holistic-scores.md`

## 1. Summary

LLP 2000 is right that the whole application is the unit of design, right
that ownership comes before abstraction, and right to ask for deterministic
simulation and an early real deployment. Its weakness is that it treats the
two structural choices that produced Snapback 2's costs as open research
questions, and then proposes a first experiment at exactly the scale where
those costs are invisible. This document takes a position on both, names
what to keep from Snapback 2 verbatim, and rewrites the first slice so it
can fail for the right reasons.

The position, in one paragraph. Snapback 2's *core* is excellent and should
be copied: the rule language and its uniformity analysis, the structural-fact
family, one data language, typed states with no silence, refusals that paste
a rewrite, personas, the successor classifier, the derived per-recipient
log, the loop verbs and their sub-second budgets. Two *substrates* under
that core are where the record shows the hours went, and both should be
flipped rather than re-investigated: (1) the static certificate should keep
certifying **authorization and shape** and stop pricing **bytes and steps**,
which move to a deterministic runtime meter with honest `capped`/abort
outcomes; and (2) the client should hold **a replica of the viewer's declared
partition** — the local-first shape every shipped sync engine and Snapback
2's own `deliver` log converge on — instead of a per-query result cache
proven by receipts. Those two flips dissolve most of the machinery that
leaked into the application (receipts, coverage, halos, validators, grants,
ID slices, drains, `withHistory`, follower inboxes, per-table retention
words) and turn the 28-second acquisition into a bulk stream whose floor is
the device's write speed. The first slice should be built on the **hub
fixture** (1,000 memberships, 500 follows, 100,000 messages), with the
day-two change designed before the day-one screen, a native client in the
first slice, and a deterministic simulator as the primary test harness.

Three claims this document makes that LLP 2000 does not:

1. **The costs have two named causes, and both are decisions, not
   mysteries.** Byte-priced static certification and the receipt-proven
   result cache account for every ergonomic residual in LLP 1018.008.009
   except documentation. §2 shows the mapping.
2. **The first experiment must include the hub.** Snapback 2 was "elegant on
   day one and hostile on day two" (LLP 1020) and broke at 1,000 memberships
   (LLPs 1023, 1024, 1025). A two-principal slice will pass and teach nothing.
3. **The process is part of the product.** Seventy-one LLPs, over two
   thousand commits, and seven ceiling raises in fourteen days produced a
   sound system nobody can hold in their head. Snapback 3 needs one owner on
   the core, a simulator instead of a test matrix, and budgets anchored to
   competitors so that raising one means admitting a loss.

## 2. What the record says, read as causes

The evidence LLP 2000 §2 cites is right; its reading is too gentle. Every
row below is a Snapback 2 cost recorded in the corpus, with the substrate
that produced it. Numbers are the corpus's own and retain its scope limits.

Against that, what scored: on the 2026-09-05 three-scorer Clique run
Snapback 2 beat Convex on authorization (82 vs 79) and offline (81 vs 44)
and lost on queries and live (60 vs 85), client integration (59 vs 79),
setup and docs (55 vs 79), diagnostics and loop (66 vs 77), operations (53
vs 76) and scale (62 vs 80); overall 66 vs 81. The later single-lane 0.0.21
and 0.0.25 scores of 82 and 85 are real improvement and not a three-scorer
comparison. The wins are the core; the losses are composition, discovery,
scale and operations — the substrates and what sits on them.

LLP 2000 §2 summarises this as "costs arise where one layer must reconstruct
another layer's facts." True, and the layer doing the reconstructing is the
client, because it was designed as a cache that may not compute. Name the
cause and the remedy follows.

## 3. Where LLP 2000 is right, and should not be diluted

- **The whole application is the unit.** §3's four properties (composition,
  locality, continuity, performance) are the right acceptance vocabulary.
  Keep them as the headings of the scenario suite.
- **Ownership before abstraction.** §5's table is the best paragraph in the
  document. §8 below turns its fourth row into a fixed vocabulary.
- **Composed reads must not fabricate.** Unknown totals stay unknown; revoked
  rows do not linger. Both flips below preserve this; they change what is
  *known*, not what is *claimed*.
- **Writes have one lifecycle with durable admission distinct from commit
  and stable operation identity.** Keep LLP 1018.004's three outcomes.
- **Rust and SQLite.** Yes, and the engine's transaction, interpreter, rule
  evaluation and successor logic are the pieces to copy first (§5).
- **Prototype the experience before the core.** Yes — and §8 makes the
  prototype's API signatures binding on the implementation, not the reverse.
- **Deterministic simulation early**, citing TigerBeetle. This is the single
  most important sentence in LLP 2000 and §11 makes it the primary harness.
- **A real deployment and a native client early.** Yes; §11 puts the native
  client in slice one.
- **Parallel, fenced, 2000-series, promotion is the author's later call.** Yes.

## 4. Where LLP 2000 is wrong or leaves the wrong things open

### 4.1 It reopens the language and leaves the bound model open; invert that

§6 asks to "evaluate Quarry" and "evaluate any alternative against the same
contracts." The one-language decision took thirty-seven paper applications,
a three-family panel, a spelling spike and an author ruling (LLP
0329.014.004 §9, LLP 1004, LLP 1007 §4b) to close, and the shipped result is
the most readable artifact in Snapback 2: the chat schema is 129 lines and a
query is three to six. Reopening the language will consume the first month.
What *should* be reopened is the bound model under it, which §6 phrases as a
comparison to "concentrate early investigation on." Half of the Quarry
refusals a builder meets are the certifier's byte and step prices wearing
Quarry syntax; the `fn`/`proc` split and the page-to-list gap (LLP 1018.008
F4) are bounded-composition restrictions the pricing model forced. Decide
the bound model (§6), keep the language, and re-derive its restrictions.

### 4.2 The first slice is at the scale where Snapback 2 looked elegant

§10 proposes "a private conversation with paginated messages and an unread
count," "two principals and two clients." Snapback 2 passed that slice in
its first week. It broke at the hub: 1,000 memberships refused the digest
fold, made global search cost a thousand requests, and refused the
envelopes builders first wrote (LLPs 1023, 1024, 1025). Every one of those

one-second margin below the lease session's five-second statement timeout.
A `57014` during the conditional claim abandons before any watcher exists.
After a successful claim, `statement_timeout` is disabled before the watcher
starts: bounded fence waits use `lock_timeout` and the finite attempt count,
so the adapter's statement timer cannot cancel a claim after signalling.
The hygiene sweep runs after COMMIT
and retains the same token bound, so a losing or delayed standby cannot
terminate a winner's sessions. Serving connections and readers carry
`sb:<32-hex-store-id>:<4-hex-holder>:<decimal-token>` (at most 60 bytes, even at
BIGINT max); oversized or malformed tag components refuse.

Fix round 1 replaces start barriers with observed blocking. The winning
standby pauses while holding its actual conditional-UPDATE lock; the loser
must appear in `pg_blocking_pids` before release. A hook inside `acquire`
renews after the expiry poll and before the conditional UPDATE, which must
return zero rows without starting a watcher. A gated watcher forces a real
`55P03`, followed by savepoint rollback; the old renewal is observed blocked
on the claimant both before and after that rollback. This fence wait also
outlives an injected 20 ms session statement timeout. The legacy opener
pauses after taking its advisory lock, and the second opener must be observed
waiting on it. A shared-advisory wait exposes a mixed blocker set while
both sessions retain owner key-shares; termination refuses while preserving
both sessions and the tagged transaction's staged write. (Postgres may expose
row multixact holders one at a time.) Evaluator refusal and a serializable
evaluator blocking legacy adoption have separate witnesses.

Physical COMMIT disables `statement_timeout`, including on lease traffic.
The adapter exposes `RuntimeError::CommitOutcomeUnknown`
(`E_COMMIT_OUTCOME_UNKNOWN`) for lost/uncertain COMMIT acknowledgements and
cancelled synchronous-replication waits. It is a store failure with automatic
retry disabled, not an execution refusal or an acknowledged success.
Explicit serialization/deadlock/constraint aborts retain their driver error.
The common engine propagates the unknown outcome without fabricating a
receipt or running a success continuation. Per-path key resolution/retry
policy remains P1a's responsibility.

`AnyStore::worker_ledger_path` preserves SQLite's adjacent completion file
and derives the Postgres completion filename from the logical store id in an
explicit absolute durable state directory. Missing identity refuses with
`E_WORKER_STORE_ID`; missing Postgres state location uses `E_WORKER_STATE`.
The existing supervisor calls this seam; configuring its Postgres location
and admission belongs to S10d-3. No URL or dummy SQLite database path is used.

Real-cluster witnesses and check results are recorded in
[the S10d-2 report](../snapback4/reports/20261022-s10d2-postgres-ownership.md).
This is a store-level slice: public StoreConfig, release/bootstrap/listener
integration, lease cadence and loss-driven admission shutdown, startup runner
policy, and worker-state configuration remain S10d-3. Declared HA modes,
provider failover qualification, database-identity/tripwire continuity and
full worker recovery remain the broader §5/P1b work; this slice claims none
of them.

#### Family dispatch and the remaining semantic boundary

Use ordinary Rust supertrait composites, with explicit implementations on
the appropriate enums. Do not construct `dyn StoreFamilies`: existing
callback methods are intentionally generic and need not be object-safe.
Each family method matches once and delegates to the corresponding adapter;
policy remains in the shared Rust above it.

**Backstop.** `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` on the serving role.
It does not replace termination, because it cannot see a backend blocked
writing to a stopped client (W7). TCP keepalives do not detect a paused
process at all.

**Ambiguous commits.** A COMMIT that races termination can be durable
while its client sees an error. Under synchronous replication that window
is seconds wide (W9). Fencing still orders it before the takeover, and a new
owner treats whatever committed as committed. The claim that every write
path is retry-safe across owners is a P1a deliverable, not an assertion.
P1a produces a per-path table: each write path (mutation, mint, refresh,
invalidation, claim, renewal, step, settle, sweep, asset view,
time-audience pin, activation), its idempotency key, and what a retry
observes in each of three outcomes (rolled back, committed and
acknowledged, committed but unacknowledged). Any path without a key gets
one; a mint is keyed by its existing mint binding. P1b's witness forces a
commit to race termination during a synchronous wait, retries the same
operation under the new owner, and asserts a single visible effect for at
least mint, claim, receipt and step.

session mode, never transaction mode. Under transaction pooling, a backend
pid and its tag belong to whichever client is mid-transaction, so

// @ref LLP 3000.009.001.000#5.4.1 — COMMIT has no adapter timeout or cancellation; loss of acknowledgement is unknown.
pub(super) fn commit(mut tx: Transaction<'_>, warning: &AtomicBool) -> Result<(), RuntimeError> {
    tx.batch_execute("SET LOCAL statement_timeout = 0; SET LOCAL lock_timeout = 0")?;
    warning.store(false, Ordering::SeqCst);
    let result = tx.commit();
    if warning.swap(false, Ordering::SeqCst) {
        return Err(RuntimeError::CommitOutcomeUnknown(
            "COMMIT returned a cancellation warning".into(),
        ));
    }
    result.map_err(|error| {
        // Explicit abort replies establish rollback. Transport loss, backend
        // termination and other unclassified COMMIT failures do not.
        if error.code().is_some_and(|code| {
            matches!(code.code(), "40001" | "40P01") || code.code().starts_with("23")
        }) {
            RuntimeError::Postgres(error)
        } else {
            RuntimeError::CommitOutcomeUnknown(error.to_string())
        }
    })
}

codex
The Postgres contract exposes another material gap: a COMMIT can be durable even when its acknowledgment fails. DX7 needs to distinguish that unknown outcome from a definite rollback, both when checkpointing an advance and when clearing the pause. Otherwise the process and durable clock state can disagree.
codex
Three material changes are required.

1. **Handle unknown database COMMIT outcomes explicitly.** [The checkpoint contract](/home/ccheever/projects/sb4-b24-dx7/llp/3000.000.000.001-staging-with-real-users.rfc.md:716) promises rollback on storage failure and retention of the pause if its final clear fails. Postgres can instead commit durably and return `E_COMMIT_OUTCOME_UNKNOWN`, as documented in [its governing contract](/home/ccheever/projects/sb4-b24-dx7/llp/3000.009.001.000-the-postgres-store-port.rfc.md:1236). A checkpoint may therefore advance credentials and durable time without publishing the process clock; an uncertain final clear may actually remove the durable pause.

   **Required:** distinguish definite rollback from unknown commit. Define how clock admission, maintenance and process-clock publication are fenced until durable state is reconciled, without replaying credential shifts. Qualify the “retain the pause” guarantee for an uncertain clear. Require fault-injection evidence for both writes.

2. **Recover from stale checkpoints, not only absent checkpoints.** [Startup recovery](/home/ccheever/projects/sb4-b24-dx7/llp/3000.000.000.001-staging-with-real-users.rfc.md:707) consults retained commit/schedule boundaries only without a checkpoint. But the explicitly permitted downgrade can leave an existing checkpoint untouched while an older binary advances time and saves later boundaries. Re-upgrading then resumes from stale metadata, potentially recreating the future-held schedule problem. Wall-clock rollback after ordinary running can produce the same mismatch.

   **Required:** include later retained boundaries in recovery even when a checkpoint exists, or detect this inconsistency and specify explicit recovery. Add checkpoint → downgrade → advance → re-upgrade coverage, plus a wall-clock rollback case.

3. **Define scroll reachability across combined clips.** [The rendering rule](/home/ccheever/projects/sb4-b24-dx7/llp/3000.000.000.001-staging-with-real-users.rfc.md:729) assumes mounted text outside an `auto/scroll` scrollport can be reached. That is not universally true: text positioned above the scrollable origin can remain unreachable at every legal scroll position. Conversely, below-fold text in an inner scrollport can become visible through an outer `overflow:hidden` container; testing its current character geometry against that outer clip rejects reachable text.

   **Required:** specify how legal scroll ranges and intervening clips compose without moving the page. Add both controls: unreachable negative-position text must remain excluded, and an inner scrollport inside an outer hidden container must admit text scrolling can reveal.

I found no additional material design blocker in the protected-immutable policy, canonical helper expansion, or gate-reporting changes. In particular, ignoring protected immutable patches for every viewer avoids an equality-based hidden-value oracle.

This was a read-only design review; I did not run qualification tests or treat unfinished implementation as a defect.
